title: Amyloidosis Continues to Fight Back
body_text: Transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis is not a disease with a particularly high profile, although it’s a very serious diagnosis indeed for the patients who have it. There’s a whole set of genetically-determined forms, but what they have in common is the production of a malfunctioning version of the transthyretin protein, which is involved in transport of both thyroxine thyroid hormone and retinol to the liver. The defective forms of the protein form amyloid deposits, and these tend to show up particularly in the peripheral nervous system or in the heart, leading to progressive and irreversible neuropathy or cardiac failure. Most commonly, it’s a single substitution of methionine for valine at position 30 of the protein, and that disrupts its usual tetrameric form. The misfolded monomers go on to cause the trouble. Traditionally the only thing to do about this is a liver transplant, which of course is a pretty tough pathway to go down (not least, in finding a compatible donor). I believe that the figures are that about 10% of the patients undergoing this treatment die from the transplant itself in one way or another, and those that survive of course have to be on immune-suppressing drugs for the rest of their lives (and that can lead to problems as well). It’s the sort of therapy you only see when the alternative is certain decline and death within a few years at most. For years there was one drug that approved to slow progression of the disease, namely tafamidis, which supposed to stabilize the protein tetramer even in people with the mutation. But it’s not as effective as anyone would like (and indeed has struggled in some clinical trials to demonstrate efficacy at all). A competitor (acoramidis) was approved in 2024. The various attempts at genetic therapy have used this disease as a proving ground, and that makes perfect sense given the state of other therapies and the clear genetic cause. Back in 2017, Alnylam made some biopharma history with a clinical success in this area using RNA interference. That drug and a follow-up have both made it on to the market (treating the abovementioned different forms of this amyloidosis). Meanwhile, AstraZeneca and their partners at Ionis have been working on an antisense oligonucleotide therapy in this area, eplontersen (brand named as Wainua). That was approved back in late 2023 for the peripheral polyneuropathy transthyretin amyloidosis, and the company has been running a Phase III of that drug against the cardiomyopathy form. Unfortunately, that one failed most thoroughly a few days ago, and it’s a failure that hardly anyone saw coming. Alnylam, as mentioned, had already shown that amyloid-directed therapy could work in this indication, and eplontersen’s data for periphera neuropathy seem pretty solid. But the drug did not reduce heart problems or outright cardiovascular deaths in the patient population. As you’ll see from that link, one possible reason is that the great majority of the patients in the trial were taking one of those two tetramer-stabilizer drugs already (since that is after all the standard of care), and perhaps there wasn’t too much room left for improvement after that? There’s a lot of second-guessing going on after this result, which was particularly unwelcome after AZ had been assuring people that their trial design was solid. But they’ve already experienced bad news with other amyloidosis plans. No idea what comes next here, but it’s an unfortunately vivid example of the complexities of such diseases- and the complexities of the therpeutic modes that we have to reach for to try to treat them.
